blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the **indices** of the two numbers that add up to `target`. Exactly one answer exists, and you may not use the same element twice.

blocks.alt: The array [2, 7, 11, 15] with target 9. The cells at index 0 and 1 are highlighted because 2 + 7 = 9, so the answer is [0, 1].

blocks.code:
Input:  nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9
Output: [0, 1]      because nums[0] + nums[1] = 2 + 7 = 9

Input:  nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6
Output: [1, 2]      3 + 3 would be 6, but that uses index 0 twice

blocks.text: The most direct idea: pick every index `i`, pair it with every later index `j`, and check whether the two values add up to `target`.

**Time O(n²), space O(1).** There are about n²/2 pairs — 5 billion for 100,000 numbers. Notice what the inner loop is really doing: for a fixed `nums[i]`, it is **searching** for one specific value, `target - nums[i]`.
2. Optimal: sort, then walk two pointers inward
Searching is faster in sorted data. Sort the array, put `left` at the smallest value and `right` at the largest, and look at their sum:

items: **Too small?** Only a bigger left value can help, so `left++`.
**Too big?** Only a smaller right value can help, so `right--`.

blocks.text: One catch: the answer needs the **original indices**, and sorting moves the values. So instead of sorting `nums`, sort a list of indices by the value they point at.
**Time O(n log n), space O(n).** The sort dominates; the pointer walk itself is only O(n). That's a huge improvement — but the sort is still work we only did to make searching cheap.
3. Best solution: one pass with a hash map

A hash map answers "have I seen this value, and where?" in **O(1)**. So walk the array once. At each number, compute the partner it needs, `need = target - nums[i]`, and ask the map whether we've already passed it. If yes, we're done. If not, store the current number so a **later** number can find it.

blocks.alt: Walking [2, 7, 11, 15] with target 9. At i = 1 the value is 7, so need = 9 − 7 = 2. The map already holds 2 → 0, so the answer is [0, 1].
blocks.caption: Each number checks the map for its partner, then adds itself for the numbers after it.

blocks.text: Storing **after** checking also takes care of the "don't use the same element twice" rule: when `nums[i]` looks for its partner, it isn't in the map yet.

blocks.caption: Try a target that needs the last two numbers, or a pair of equal values like [3, 3].

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** Every number is visited once and each map lookup is O(1) on average. We spend memory on the map to save time — the classic trade.

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n²) time, O(1) space. Optimal: O(n log n) time, O(n) space. Best: O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: **Equal values** — `[3, 3]`, target 6 returns `[0, 1]`. The first 3 is stored before the second one looks for it.
**Don't reuse an element** — `[3, 2, 4]`, target 6 returns `[1, 2]`, not `[0, 0]`.
**The pair is at the very end** — the loop must reach the last index.
